goal: Bake my first sourdough loaf this weekend; my starter is already active
interpretation: The learner bakes a decent first sourdough boule this weekend with their active starter, understanding each step (levain, hydration, bulk, shaping, cold proof, scoring, Dutch oven bake) from at most two consistent bakers.
assumptions: The 'weekend' bake means mixing Friday/Saturday, a cold retard overnight, and baking the next day, so a 1-2 day timeline is acceptable.
The learner owns or can get a Dutch oven, a kitchen scale, and a banneton or a bowl with a towel.
The learner wants a standard country-style white or lightly whole-wheat boule at around 70-75% hydration, not an advanced high-hydration loaf.
Since 'at most two bakers' methods' is required, the plan favors one primary full bake-along baker plus one optional secondary for troubleshooting.

sub_topics.title: Hydration and building a levain from an active starter
sub_topics.why: They know yeasted dough but not baker's percentages or how to turn a starter into a levain that fits the weekend schedule.

sub_topics.title: Mixing, autolyse, and bulk fermentation with stretch-and-folds
sub_topics.why: Yeast timing cues do not apply; they must learn to read dough (volume increase, bubbles, jiggle) instead of the clock, and replace kneading with folds.

sub_topics.title: Pre-shaping and shaping a boule with surface tension
sub_topics.why: Sandwich-loaf shaping is different; wetter sourdough needs tension-building technique to hold its shape.

sub_topics.title: Final proof and cold retard in the fridge
sub_topics.why: Makes the weekend schedule workable and develops flavor; they need to know how to judge proofing with the poke test and avoid overproofing.

sub_topics.title: Scoring and baking in a preheated Dutch oven
sub_topics.why: Dutch oven steam and scoring control oven spring and crust, which they have never done with sandwich bread.

sub_topics.title: Follow a full beginner sourdough bake-along from start to finish
sub_topics.why: Ties all steps together into one consistent method so the learner can follow along at the counter.

sub_topics.title: Common beginner sourdough mistakes and fixes
sub_topics.why: Helps diagnose dense crumb, flat loaves, sticking dough, and underproofing/overproofing on a first bake.

picks.title: Your First Sourdough Bread (FULL COURSE in 30 minutes)
picks.reason: This is a full beginner bake-along that goes from levain and hydration through bulk with stretch-and-folds, shaping, cold retard, scoring and the Dutch oven bake. It explains the why of each step and ends with crumb troubleshooting. It works as the single recipe to follow this weekend, and it suits a yeast baker who needs the sourdough-specific steps.

evidence.quote: you will learn how to make the perfect sourdough bread at home. It has nice oven spring, it features a crisp crust, it's soft on the inside.
with slightly wet hands, I am checking the dough now. And see this, exactly what I promised you. You developed this amazing gluten network simply by waiting.
I'm going to be using a banneton like this, but you could also just use a bowl with a kitchen towel inside.

picks.confidence_note: Content and level fit well. The segment timestamps run past the stated duration, so the exact timing of sections is uncertain.

picks.title: 18 Sourdough Basics YOU Should Know
picks.reason: The same baker explains hydration levels, water ratios, fermentolyse, stretch-and-fold timing and how to know bulk fermentation is done. This fills in the hydration and fermentation concepts you lack, using the same method as the main bake-along. It is flagged surface_intro, but the unflagged course gives less depth on these concepts and no other creator is needed.

evidence.quote: less water equals happier yeast and happier baker when you're making a sourdough starter
knowing when your fermentation is done is the secret to mastering sourdough bread

picks.confidence_note: Lower confidence because of the surface_intro flag and overlap with the course. Raise it if you want extra depth on hydration and bulk readiness; skip it if you feel confident after the course.

picks.title: The ONLY SOURDOUGH BREAD SHAPING Tutorial You Will Ever Need
picks.reason: A dedicated demo of shaping with surface tension, including banneton prep with rice flour and a simple beginner roll-and-pull method. Shaping is hard to learn from a fast bake-along, so this adds a closer look from the same baker without changing methods.

evidence.quote: you're trying to pull your dough together to create a lot of tension this tension will later on result in oven spring
rice flour is advised it's going to absorb a lot more humidity so sprinkle your banneton with a little bit of rice flour

picks.confidence_note: Clear, on-topic and from the same creator. It carries a surface_intro flag, but a short focused technique demo is what is wanted here.

picks.title: What creates the BEST OPEN CRUMB? Cold proofing or Room temperature?
picks.reason: Shows pre-shaping, the finger poke test, and baking with the lid on in a Dutch oven for steam, then compares a cold-retarded loaf with a room-temperature one. This gives the cold retard and scoring detail the course covers only briefly. It is the same baker, so there are no contradictions.

evidence.quote: letting this one sit at room temperature until it passes the finger poke test
baking now for 25 minutes at 230 degrees celsius lid covered so that there's a lot of steam

picks.confidence_note: The video is tagged intermediate, and its segment map runs past the stated duration. Follow the cold-retard branch, not the room-temperature loaf.

picks.title: 10 Mistakes Beginner Sourdough Bakers Make
picks.reason: Walks through ten beginner mistakes, including bulk fermentation errors, weak shaping, scoring and oven temperature, and says to skip the cold ferment only at the cost of flavor. It is the second baker and is used only for troubleshooting, not as a second recipe. It addresses the steps beginners get wrong.

evidence.quote: Bulk fermentation is probably the hardest step for most new bakers, and it's honestly just takes a little bit of time and understanding how your dough should feel
Shaping isn't about making your dough pretty. It's about giving it the structure to spring up in the oven instead of spreading out flat
The cold ferment or cold proof is one of the easiest ways to really level up your bread. This happens after we have completed bulk fermentation

picks.confidence_note: Strong match for the mistakes slot. Some of its advice may differ from the first baker's method; where it does, stay with the first baker.
